explanations.explanation: That's the word. Paul, the apostle who wrote this letter to the believers in Rome, says he tells them this mystery “so that you will not be conceited”. Earlier he had already told the Gentiles not to boast over the branches (Romans 11:18). I think this mystery is a good cure for a swelled head.

Close to a feeling, but not the one Paul names. He says he wants them not to be conceited. Discouraged is more my speed, since I spent years being discouraged in a junk drawer. Paul's warning is about bragging, and he had already said not to boast over the branches (Romans 11:18).

Paul doesn't use that word here. He says he doesn't want them to be conceited. Nothing in this verse mentions the church splitting up. Keep your eye on that word conceited, because Paul says the mystery is given so they won't be that.
Yes, baker. Paul says, “A hardening in part has come to Israel…” Notice the words in part. It's not the whole story, and Paul says it lasts only until the full number of the Gentiles has come in.

Scattering is a good guess for a story about Israel, but it's not what Paul says. He says a hardening has come to Israel in part. Scattering isn't anywhere in these verses. Hardening is the word, and it comes with a time limit.

Nope, Paul doesn't say anything about a silence. The word is hardening, and he says it has come to Israel in part. Then he tells how long it lasts: until the full number of the Gentiles has come in. If you ask me, that's a lot of information for one verse.

This one's a trap, friend, and the trap is the word forever. Paul says the hardening has come “until the full number of the Gentiles has come in.” An until means it has an end. He doesn't say it lasts forever.

That's right. Paul says the hardening has come in part, “until the full number of the Gentiles has come in.” That's a time limit, not a forever. Then in the next verse he goes straight to all Israel being saved.

That's the big one. Paul says, “And so all Israel will be saved…” It fits what he asked earlier, when he said God has not rejected His people (Romans 11:1). I think that's good news worth reading twice.

Forgotten isn't in Paul's vocabulary here. He says all Israel will be saved. Earlier he asked if God had rejected His people and answered, “Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1). I know a little about being forgotten, and Paul is not describing that.

Cut off sounds like the branches Paul talked about earlier, but that's not his big statement here. He says all Israel will be saved. He had already asked whether God rejected His people and said, “Certainly not!” (Romans 11:1). So this verse lands on the other side of that.

Yes, baker. The Scripture goes on, “And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins.” Notice the when. The covenant is tied to God taking their sins away. Paul is quoting the prophet Isaiah here (Isaiah 59:20-21).

This one is actually true, so it's easy to trip on. The quote continues, “And this is My covenant with them when I take away their sins.” So the covenant comes with God taking away their sins. Paul is quoting the prophet Isaiah here (Isaiah 59:20-21).

That's right. Paul says that regarding election, they are loved on account of the patriarchs. He has just said that regarding the gospel they are enemies on the Gentiles' account. So he's showing two sides, and this is the loved side.

Priests are a fair guess for an Israel question, but Paul doesn't name them. He says regarding election they are loved on account of the patriarchs. It's one side of a two-sided picture. The other side is that regarding the gospel they are enemies on the Gentiles' account.

Kings are a natural guess, but Paul doesn't mention them here. He says regarding election they are loved on account of the patriarchs. That's the second side of two. The first side is that regarding the gospel they are enemies on the Gentiles' account.
Paul says the exact opposite, baker. He writes, “For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable.” Irrevocable means God doesn't take them back. That's why the loved side of Israel still stands.

Right. Paul says, “For God’s gifts and His call are irrevocable.” Irrevocable is a big word that means they can't be called back. I once got a refund on a bag of chocolate chips, but God's gifts don't work like that.

That's it. Paul says, “Just as you who formerly disobeyed God have now received mercy through their disobedience…” So the Gentiles in Rome received mercy through Israel's disobedience. It's a surprising turn, and Paul just says it plainly.

Faithfulness sounds like the nice answer, but it isn't the word Paul uses. He says the Gentiles received mercy through Israel's disobedience. Paul is describing how the two groups are connected, and the word is disobedience.

Sacrifices aren't mentioned in these verses. Paul says the Gentiles in Rome received mercy through Israel's disobedience. That's the word the verse gives. Sacrifices are a fine thing to wonder about, but they aren't what he's talking about here.

explanations.answer: The mercy shown to the Gentiles
explanations.explanation: That's right. Paul says they too have now disobeyed, “in order that they too may now receive mercy through the mercy shown to you.” It goes both ways. Mercy came to the Gentiles through Israel's disobedience, and now mercy comes to Israel through the mercy shown to the Gentiles.

Moses, Israel's leader, is a big name, but Paul doesn't bring him up here. He says Israel may receive mercy through the mercy shown to the Gentiles. The law isn't part of this verse. Paul is tracing mercy going back and forth between two groups.

Prophets matter a lot in this passage, since Paul quotes Isaiah. But he doesn't say mercy comes through their prayers. He says Israel receives mercy through the mercy shown to the Gentiles. That's the loop he describes.

Yes, baker. Paul says, “For God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone.” Notice that it says everyone twice. This is his summary after explaining how Gentiles and Israel both come to mercy.

This one is actually true. Paul says, “For God has consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone.” The word everyone shows up twice. It's the summary of the whole back-and-forth he's been describing.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, “How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!” Unsearchable and untraceable. Paul doesn't offer a study plan that gets you to the bottom of it.

Right. Paul says, “How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!” Those two words, unsearchable and untraceable, say it clearly. I've read a lot of recipes, but even I can't trace out the ways of God.

That's the answer he's after. Paul asks, “Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?” The questions are meant to be answered with no one. He is quoting the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 40:13).

Prophets are a reasonable guess, especially since Paul is quoting one, Isaiah, a prophet of Israel (Isaiah 40:13). But Paul's questions are asking who has known the mind of the Lord, and he expects the answer no one. The questions work as a way of saying that no one has.

Paul is an apostle himself, he says so in Romans 11:13, and he's the one asking the questions. So I think he isn't counting himself in. The questions ask who has known the mind of the Lord or been His counselor, and the answer he expects is no one.

It goes the other way, baker. Paul quotes the question, “Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?” It's asked as a question that expects no one. Then in the next verse he says all things are from Him and through Him and to Him.

That's right. The quote from the book of Job asks, “Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?” (Job 41:11). It expects the answer no one, so there's no one God owes. Paul follows it with, “For from Him and through Him and to Him are all things.”
That's right. Paul says, “To Him be the glory forever! Amen.” He has just said that from Him and through Him and to Him are all things. So the glory goes to God.

Israel has been the main subject of this whole passage, so it's a fair guess. But Paul says the glory goes to Him, meaning God, who all things are from, through and to. Israel is loved, but the glory goes to God forever.

The church gets plenty of attention in this letter, but Paul doesn't give it the glory. He says all things are from Him and through Him and to Him, and then, “To Him be the glory forever! Amen.” The glory goes to God.
